2 · Paste the post copy

One sentence in federal law says the grid reliability rules don't apply to Alaska. Executive Order 14421 carries no sentence like it.

The order borrows the statute's definition of the bulk-power system almost word for word. It adds a threshold the statute never had at 69,000 volts. The Alaska Energy Authority puts the Alaska Intertie at 138 kilovolts and calls it part of the interconnected Bulk Electrical System. The Railbelt Reliability Council calls the same grid islanded.

DOE takes written comments through October 9th, 2026. Its rules are due 120 days from the order.

Both definitions sit side by side in the deck at identical size, and the order's stated reason names data centers and artificial intelligence.

Which Alaska institution should put the Railbelt's voltages in front of DOE before that window closes?

#AlaskaEnergy #Railbelt #BulkPowerSystem

3 · Post, then paste this as the FIRST comment (within a minute)

Editor's note

SHIPS at 8.47 against a threshold of 8.3, no hard fails, not rounded. The round-1 cap was slide 06's headline at 4.0:1 on the pier's lit face; it now sits on a shaded form board and both progress counters sit in their own struck fields. Verified two ways: machine_qa carries ZERO contrast warns deck-wide, down from three, and slides 01 and 06 return no warns of any kind.

Read slide 04, then 08, then 07 before posting. 04 is the whole argument and the frame most likely to be misread, and nothing in a comment should say Alaska is excluded or included, because C12 is an absence claim at 0.85 confidence. 08 is what keeps the deck from reading as an accusation and is the answer to the inevitable objection that the order obviously covers Alaska, so answer with that slide rather than with a position. 07 carries every number anyone will screenshot.

MEASURED AFTER THE SCORER WROTE THIS. shrink_pdfs.py ran at Phase 11 and DECLINED to resample, which is the correct outcome and not a failure. Every candidate image scored 35.9 to 40.1 dB PSNR against a 42 dB floor, because this deck's art is high-frequency spangle, stipple and grain, which is exactly what a 192 to 144 DPI resample destroys. The shipped file is 35.37 MiB, over the 2 to 25 MB band. LinkedIn's document limit is well above that, so the upload is fine and the band is a house target rather than a platform one. The scorer's sentence below was a projection written before the measurement and is left in place unedited.

Known and accepted, not oversights: slide 03's rubber stamp is a raster, so it is invisible to the LinkedIn ranker and to accessibility, which is documented in the reconciliation; one page rule on slide 02 still lands on the body's third line at the baseline, a warn rather than a strike-through; C02, the order's title, and C11, the 180 day acquisition line, are verified and deliberately unprinted, so do not add either in a comment.

For the NEXT deck rather than this one: artwork craft is the weakest criterion at 6 and carries the largest weight in the rubric. Four defects still stand, slide 07's empty board middle, slide 06's featureless sky and bead insulators, slide 02's apron still reading as stucco, and the single declared plywood bench rendering as three different materials across 04, 08 and 10. No slide climbed the rendered ladder in this run.
Read slide 04, slide 08 and slide 07 before posting.

Slide 04 is the deck's whole argument and the frame most likely to be misread. It sets the statute's definition and the order's definition at identical size, measure and colour, and the only difference drawn is a gold line under the right column. The missing Alaska sentence in Executive Order 14421 is drawn as an absence of ink, never as a deletion, because C12 is an absence claim at 0.85 confidence. Nothing on that frame says Alaska is excluded or included, and nothing should be added in a comment that does.

Slide 08 is the counterweight and it is what keeps this deck from reading as an accusation. The Alaska Energy Authority calls the Alaska Intertie an integral part of the interconnected Bulk Electrical System (C31), which cuts toward the order reaching Alaska, and it is given the same page size and the same highlighter length as the Railbelt Reliability Council's word islanded (C24). If a reader takes the deck as a claim that Alaska is out, that slide is the answer, and the equality is measurable rather than asserted.

Slide 07 carries every number someone will screenshot. The DeepGreen row is phantom-dashed and labelled PROPOSED because Project No. 15423-000 is a preliminary permit and not a built line (C37, C38). The ladder is linear in kilovolts against a printed scale, so the distance between 138 kV and the order's 69 kV is measured rather than claimed. One string on that slide compresses two sources. The foot reads that five utilities run nearly 700 miles between those towns, where the council's own wording is five load-serving utilities interconnected across nearly 700 miles (C26, C28) and the four towns come from its footprint description (C25). If a Railbelt engineer pushes on that sentence, quote the council's wording back.

FOUR THINGS THE BUILD CHANGED against the storyboard, all of them in copy that actually rendered, so the strings here are the render and not the dossier. Slide 05's body was rewritten, the four quoted categories now live in the four struck rows and the body attributes the supporting critical infrastructure qualifier to the order rather than stating it flat. Slide 07's ladder rows were retitled and its strip caption folded into the foot, so a separate five utilities line no longer exists as its own string. Slide 08's foot now says the council SAYS it serves nearly three-quarters of Alaskans, which attributes C27 on the slide as the hedge list requires. Slide 09 dropped the 180 day Federal Acquisition Regulation line, so C11 is verified in claims.json and prints nowhere in the deck, and the tag now carries only the 120 day rule deadline.

Nothing in the locked caption reads as a factual error against claims.json. The 120 day line matches C10, the October 9th, 2026 date matches C16, and both Alaska Energy Authority phrases match C30 and C31 word for word.

PDF SIZE35.37 MiB shipped, above the 2 to 25 MB house band. shrink_pdfs.py declined the resample on a 42 dB PSNR floor and that is the right call. Fixing it is a Phase 5 decision on the NEXT deck, build from broad modelled form rather than dense fine noise, and not a problem to patch at ship.
GAS WATCHgaswatch_pagecheck reports 1 missing record, first 2026-09-08. There was no routine run that day. The series is written by .github/workflows/gaswatch.yml and never by a run, so a run can't backfill it and CINGSA keeps no archive to rebuild from. Reported here rather than repaired.

Aftercare (this is where reach is won)

  • Post Tuesday through Thursday between 8 a.m. and 11 a.m. Alaska time, and get it out well ahead of October 9th, 2026 (C16), because the close asks a reader to act inside a comment window that shuts that day.
  • Paste the sources comment within 60 seconds of posting, straight from the block above and unedited, so every raw govinfo and uscode.house.gov URL lands as plain text a reader can copy.
  • Stay on the post for the first 90 minutes and answer every comment with a claim id, a voltage or a date, never a thank you on its own.
  • Expect the objection that the order obviously reaches Alaska, and answer it with slide 08 rather than a position. Nobody has said Alaska is in and nobody has said Alaska is out, which is the deck's whole point.
  • Note saves and comments at 48 hours against the last four decks, and write down whether the two identical columns on slide 04 or the voltage ladder on slide 07 was the frame people quoted back.
